title: Comprehensions
summary: A comprehension is a short way to build a new list from a sequence of values.
introduction: A comprehension is a short way to build a new list from a sequence of values. First read the longer loop version. Then see how the short version does the same job, such as doubling each score in a list.
learningObjectives: Rewrite an append-in-a-loop as a list comprehension
Filter items with an if clause and transform them with a conditional expression
Build dictionaries and sets with comprehension syntax
Use generator expressions to feed sum(), max() and any() without a temporary list

blocks.title: squares.py
blocks.code:
numbers = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]

squares = []
for n in numbers:
    squares.append(n * n)
print(squares)

squares = [n * n for n in numbers]
print(squares)

names = ["ada", "grace", "linus"]
print([name.title() for name in names])
print([len(name) for name in names])

blocks.text: Read `[n * n for n in numbers]` starting at the `for`: for each `n` in `numbers`, produce `n * n`, and collect the results in a new list. The expression before the `for` is what goes into the list; it can be anything, including a method call or an f-string. The loop version and the comprehension produce identical results; the comprehension simply says it in one line and avoids the empty-list-then-append ceremony.

blocks.title: filtering.py
blocks.code:
numbers = range(1, 11)

evens = [n for n in numbers if n % 2 == 0]
print(evens)

big_squares = [n * n for n in numbers if n * n > 50]
print(big_squares)

labels = ["even" if n % 2 == 0 else "odd" for n in range(1, 5)]
print(labels)

words = ["apple", "Bob", "cat", "Dune"]
print([w.lower() for w in words if w[0].isupper()])

blocks.text: An `if` *after* the `for` filters: items that fail the test are skipped and nothing is produced for them. A conditional expression *before* the `for` chooses what to produce for every item, and nothing is skipped. The two can be combined, but if a comprehension needs both plus a long expression, a plain loop is clearer.

Curly braces with a `key: value` expression build a dictionary; curly braces with a single expression build a set. Both accept the same `for` and `if` clauses, and both are the quickest way to reshape data: index a list by some field, convert units, invert a mapping.

blocks.title: dict_set.py

blocks.text: When two items produce the same key, the later one wins, which is why `inverted` maps `6` to `cherry` and `banana` has disappeared. That is a feature when you want the last value and a bug when you do not; check for duplicate keys before inverting a mapping.

blocks.title: nested.py
blocks.code:
pairs = [(x, y) for x in range(1, 4) for y in range(1, 3)]
print(pairs)

matrix = [[1, 2, 3], [4, 5, 6]]
flat = [value for row in matrix for value in row]
print(flat)

transposed = [[row[i] for row in matrix] for i in range(3)]
print(transposed)

blocks.text: Two `for` clauses behave like nested loops, written in the same order as the loops would be: the first `for` is the outer loop, so `x` changes slowly and `y` quickly. A comprehension *inside* a comprehension builds a list of lists, as `transposed` does. These are the limit of readable nesting; beyond that, write a function with ordinary loops.

blocks.title: Readable beats clever
blocks.text: A comprehension that needs scrolling, three conditions or a side effect such as calling `print` inside it has stopped being a comprehension and become a puzzle. If you cannot say what it does in one sentence, write the loop. A `for` loop also states honestly that you want the side effects rather than the list, which a comprehension used for its side effects hides.

Parentheses instead of brackets create a **generator expression**: it produces items one at a time as the consumer asks for them, so `sum()` can add a million squares without ever holding a million-item list in memory. When the generator is the only argument to a function, its own parentheses can be dropped.

blocks.title: generators.py
blocks.code:
numbers = range(1, 1_000_001)

total = sum(n * n for n in numbers)
print(total)

print(max(len(word) for word in ["kiwi", "banana", "fig"]))
print(any(n > 999_000 for n in numbers))
print(all(n > 0 for n in numbers))

squares = (n * n for n in range(5))
print(type(squares).__name__)
print(list(squares))
print(list(squares))      # exhausted: a generator can be consumed once

blocks.text: `any()` stops at the first true value and `all()` at the first false one, so combined with a generator they do the minimum work. A generator can be consumed only once: the second `list(squares)` is empty because the first call used everything up. If you need the items twice, build a list.

blocks.title: Try it
blocks.text: Given `words = ["Python", "is", "fun"]`, write one comprehension that returns the words longer than two letters in upper case, and a dict comprehension that maps each word to its first letter.

questions.question: Which comprehension produces `[0, 2, 4, 6]`?
questions.explanation: `range(4)` yields 0, 1, 2, 3 and doubling each gives 0, 2, 4, 6. The `if n % 2` version keeps the odd numbers, and `range(1, 4)` skips 0.
options: `[n for n in range(8) if n % 2]`

questions.question: A generator expression such as `(n * n for n in range(5))` creates the whole list of results in memory immediately.
questions.explanation: A generator produces values lazily, one at a time, as they are requested. Only a list comprehension with square brackets builds the full list up front.

seo.title: Python Comprehensions – List, Dict, Set and Generators
seo.description: Learn Python list, dict and set comprehensions with conditions and nesting, and generator expressions that feed sum(), max() and any() without a temporary list.
